speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Energy Market Authority of Singapore (EMA) Act, Electricity Act and Gas Act underpin the energy market structure and regulatory framework we have today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Electricity and Gas Acts establish the regulatory regimes to ensure competitive, secure and reliable electricity and gas supply to the industry and the public.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Yesterday, I spoke about the pre-emptive measures that EMA will be taking to safeguard Singapore’s energy security in the near term to address the recent supply crunch and volatility in global energy markets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: However, energy security is not just about ensuring the robustness of our current energy supply.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is also about looking into our energy future.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MTI and EMA have embarked on a multi-decade programme to decarbonise our power sector.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will need to make a shift on many aspects – reducing greenhouse gas emissions from existing power plants, maximising solar deployment, working with our regional partners to develop renewable energy sources and developing new low-carbon alternatives.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We should not underestimate how challenging this journey will be.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Some countries are experiencing an energy crunch because they have not provided sufficient safeguards and contingencies for their transition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This Bill will provide EMA with three important powers to secure our electricity supply over this transition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are proposing to update the relevant Acts in three key areas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Second, to enhance the protection of critical electricity and gas infrastructure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And third, to empower EMA to impose energy and carbon efficiency on parties licensed under the Electricity Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Safeguarding energy security and reliability – first, I will speak on our amendments to ensure that we have a safe, secure and reliable supply of electricity which is critical to Singapore’s survival.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Today, we rely on the private sector to provide sufficient generation capacity and the critical infrastructure needed for energy security and system stability.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: However, the global energy transition introduces various risks and uncertainties in energy markets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For example, it is unclear when new energy solutions, such as hydrogen and carbon capture, utilisation and storage may become cost-viable for large-scale deployment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is also unclear how natural gas may feature in the future global energy mix.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For example, generation companies may not be willing to invest in new generation capacity to replace older retiring generation units.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They may also not be willing to invest in new technologies that incorporate cleaner fuel.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Banks may be increasingly reluctant to finance generation projects which are needed but are not based on renewable energy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To safeguard energy reliability and security during the energy transition, we must give EMA the option to step in and provide the critical infrastructure and services needed to ensure the proper functioning of the energy sector.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Examples of such infrastructure would be generating units, energy storage solutions and transmission infrastructure, including those that may be required for cross-border electricity trading.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This will allow EMA to provide the required critical infrastructure when there is a need to do so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: One example is the Open Cycle Gas Turbines (OCGT).

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: OCGTs are quick response units that can be brought online quickly to augment any shortfall in generation capacity, such as when there are unplanned outages among other generation units.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These quick response units are necessary for the security and reliability of our electricity system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: However, there is little private sector interest to build these units as they are less competitive compared to the Combined Cycle Gas Turbines.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The existing OCGTs in Singapore are more than 30 years old and they are long overdue for replacement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: EMA could step in to build new OCGTs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Where needed, EMA may directly operate the critical infrastructure or set up a subsidiary to do so.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Should EMA or its subsidiary operate the critical infrastructure, operational Key Performance Indicators, or KPIs, similar to the regulatory requirements that licensees are subjected to today, will be imposed, in lieu of licensing requirements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Bill also expands EMA’s borrowing powers in the EMA Act to allow EMA to issue bonds, in addition to borrowing through commercial or Government loans, to finance the construction of these critical infrastructure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In EMA’s industry consultations, power generation companies were concerned that the units that would be owned and operated by EMA would compete with their units in the wholesale electricity market and depress wholesale electricity prices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There were also concerns that EMA would act as both regulator and owner/operator of the generation unit.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: First, this amendment is worded broadly to provide EMA with the flexibility to react to the wide range of scenarios which may undermine the security, stability and reliability of our energy sector.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our preference is for the private sector to build, own and operate the electricity infrastructure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Second, EMA will be putting in place safeguards to ensure that they do not compete unfairly against the private generation companies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For example, EMA may set up a separate subsidiary to own and operate a generating unit and will put in place proper procedures and governance structures to mitigate any conflict of interests.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is needed to enhance protection of critical electricity and gas infrastructure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Currently, sections 80 and 85 of the Electricity Act, and sections 32, 32A and 32B of the Gas Act, only penalise offenders who damage the actual cables and pipelines.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: However, as the infrastructure housing these cables are an important part of the transmission network, EMA will be expanding the scope of the offences in these sections to cover such protective infrastructure as well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The offences carry the same penalties as those for damaging the actual cables and pipelines.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Currently, around 95% of our electricity is generated using natural gas, which is the cleanest form of fossil fuel.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Even as we ramp up various sources of low carbon energy, such as solar energy and tap on regional power grids for low carbon energy, natural gas will remain an important source of energy for us over the next few decades.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To reduce the carbon footprint of electricity generation, it is important that we gradually shift towards cleaner and more efficient modes of power generation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Under clause 3(k), these policies and strategies may be imposed on licensees through Codes of Practices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This move towards a reduction of greenhouse gas emissions is part of a larger effort to shape a more energy- and carbon-efficient power sector.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To date, more than half of the larger generation companies have tapped on the grant to make improvements to their generation units.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: However, as low carbon technology matures and becomes more cost-competitive, it is timely and necessary for the sector to move beyond incentives and grants and to empower EMA to regulate on this front.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: EMA will work with the industry to develop reasonable standards and provide a transition period for existing generation units as needed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This amendment will also complement ongoing economy-wide initiatives to lower carbon emissions, such as carbon taxes, to transition the power sector towards low carbon generation sources.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Bill also makes several miscellaneous amendments to the Electricity, Gas and EMA Acts and related amendments to the District Cooling Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These include streamlining the licence application and extension process for all electricity and gas licensees, clarifying the prudential obligations of specified licensees in the event of an insolvency situation, clarifying inspection obligations in connection with gas installations and updating key terms and definitions in the Electricity Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have made ambitious commitments to reduce our carbon emissions and combat climate change, but the developments unfolding around the world also serve as a stark reminder of the complexity of this transition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As energy forms the bedrock of our economy and our society, it is especially important for Singapore to manage the transition well and seamlessly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In finalising these amendments, MTI and EMA had sought feedback from industry stakeholders and members of the public through a public consultation exercise earlier this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MTI and EMA have carefully considered all feedback received and incorporated them where relevant.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This Bill is necessary to ensure that EMA has the necessary levers to navigate the energy transition, while ensuring that our energy supply remains secure and reliable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: My Ministry will also continue to monitor and study further enhancements to legislation to facilitate a smoother energy transition while safeguarding Singapore's energy security, reliability and affordability.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: One, for EMA to safeguard energy security; and two, to enable EMA to implement policies to reduce carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Energy prices are surging in the global markets due to a combination of factors: supply crunch, weather, soaring demand and geopolitical tensions and so on.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And this would soon translate into higher electricity prices to consumers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It does not help that a number of the electricity retailers, also impacted by the recent price volatility and have exited at this time, leaving thousands of households who have subscribed to the fixed plan exposed to the impending hike in electricity prices.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Adding to the uncertainties, the imported piped natural gas from Indonesia is also disrupted, leading to EMA taking the extraordinary pre-emptive steps to establish standby fuel facilities where power generation companies or gencos can draw upon.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Beyond the current energy woes, the longer-term challenge for Singapore would be how we can repower ourselves as almost all the existing natural gas-powered plants will reach the end of their shelf life and would be retired in the next one to two decades.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: What would be the new mix of energy sources in the future that will be both efficient and resilient and also meet our sustainability goals?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is a key strategic policy decision the Government has to make and to implement.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But this major transition to a more efficient, resilient and sustainable energy architecture for Singapore also requires new executive powers to effect massive industry changes and restructuring.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In situations of crisis or significant market disruption, EMA may require this delegation of authority to take necessary decisive actions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I will go further to submit that critical infrastructures like power generation which has a direct bearing on our security, economy and the well-being of our people should be a nationalised company or maybe even Temasek-linked companies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This would ensure that the power generation companies would be operated and invested with our long-term national interest in mind.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is especially so for a small island economy like Singapore, where we lack the scale.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Power generation infrastructures do have their useful lifespan and obsolescence.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It requires continuous long-term investments to renew, repower and invest in new capacities to meet our growth demands.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There is now also the added sustainability emphasis as well as the need for further resiliency to be built into our future energy supply.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Whilst doing all the above, we also want to ensure that electricity prices stay affordable to consumers and to businesses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: All these requirements and often competing needs may not be best served by commercially-run business enterprises.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Having these infrastructures largely owned and operated by, say, foreign commercial entities, may leave us exposed to potential disruptions should the parent head offices or other subsidiaries of these companies run into problems or that they have no plans to reinvest and merely want to sit out the legacy investment till it is fully depreciated.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Of course, the Government can regulate to require the gencos to close the line, but we know that too much of regulations and directives can actually kill the enterprising spirit and defeat the purpose.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The other steep challenge faced by power generation companies is the ability of the company to fund the long-term capital expenditure needed to renew and to grow the capacity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Not all companies are able to raise long-term capital which can stretch more than 10 years or 20 years, at a reasonable cost.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is needed to facilitate the decarbonisation of our gencos and, importantly, it signals the way forward in how we generate electricity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Besides enabling EMA to push for carbon-efficient technologies through this Bill, there are also the upcoming carbon taxes to incentivise the reduction of carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In recent years, we have seen more forward-looking businesses incorporating sustainability into their corporate agenda.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hence, rather than use the powers derived from this Bill to institute broad-based measures, I would suggest that EMA can look at more targeted measures to move the sector towards lower emissions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: With the progressive build-up of the four supply "switches" and the diversification of the various energy sources, the regulations and the development of the sector would also need a more differentiated approach.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In particular, whether hydrogen, which has been quite talked about, can be a viable source or game changer for Singapore energy supply; and also, what would be the likely timeline?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As EMA embarks on this multi-decade programme to transit to a low-carbon, four-supply switches setting, it would, understandably, change the overall market dynamics of the incumbent operators.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Some of these new plans may directly or indirectly impact the operations and financial performances of these players.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This may be just the tip of the iceberg of people affected by increasing electricity prices.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This indicates that lower-income Singaporeans may be disproportionately impacted by higher electricity prices.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Other households which have locked in lower rates in their retail contracts will soon face their day of reckoning when they renew their contracts, as the new rates will reflect the higher prevailing electricity prices.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This electricity price hike could not have come at a worse time for many households.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our economy has yet to fully recover from the pandemic-induced downturn and many Singaporeans are still struggling with job losses, salary reductions and disrupted careers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many are working and studying from home, resulting in higher household electricity usage.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This should be on top of existing U-Save rebates, which were calculated before the current electricity price increases occurred.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I appreciate Minister Tan See Leng's reply yesterday that he is exploring with MOF further means to help and is working out the details with them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The current electricity price increase can be traced to disruptions in the supply of natural gas to Singapore and higher demand globally.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In the last few months, the curtailment of the flow of gas from Indonesia's West Natuna gas field and the lower landing pressure of gas supplied from South Sumatra has severely impacted a vital source of our power generation needs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Energy (Resilience Measures and Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill that is before the House today is timely, as it seeks to better safeguard Singapore's energy security.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It enables the Energy Market Authority (EMA) to construct, acquire, manage and protect electricity infrastructure and authorises EMA to implement policies to reduce the emission of greenhouse gases in the generation of electricity.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is comforting to know that EMA will be able to step in to build, own and operate power generation plants, if needed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, in practice, will this be done only as a last resort, for example, if existing gencos fail in their roles?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Or is EMA already making plans to directly build and operate critical electricity infrastructure like undersea cables to import electricity from overseas?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I note the Minister just said in his Second Reading speech that the Government's preference is for the private sector to build, own and operate electricity infrastructure and that, before exercising this power, EMA will explore the other options available.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Minister has also assured the House that EMA will put in place Government structures to mitigate conflicts of interest.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can he elaborate on what these Government structures will be to ensure fair competition in the electricity market and mitigate conflicts of interest?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government has announced plans to embark on a multi-decade programme to transition our electricity generation to low-carbon generation sources through four supply switches.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These are: first, by increasing energy efficiency of natural gas power plants; second, by accelerating solar deployment; third, by tapping on regional power grids for low-carbon electricity imports; and, fourth, by developing low-carbon solutions, such as hydrogen and carbon capture utilisation and storage (CCUS).

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: About 95% of our electricity is generated from imported natural gas.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is unusually high compared to other countries and it carries concentration risks.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Recently, the tiny European nation of Moldova, which gets almost all its gas from Russia, had to declare a state of emergency over a gas shortage.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Russian state gas giant, Gazprom, hiked its prices four-fold, then reduced supply when Moldova refused to pay.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Moscow has been accused of weaponising its gas monopoly in Moldova, which recently elected a pro-Western president and parliament.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In Singapore, around 70% of our natural gas is piped from Malaysia and Indonesia.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Will we face similar threats should relations with our neighbours get rocky, as they do from time to time?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In fact, it may already be happening, even in the absence of diplomatic problems.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In February 2020, the Indonesian government announced that it intends to halt gas exports to Singapore by 2023, when one of our two gas pipeline contracts expires.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This ought to set off alarm bells, given our heavy reliance on Indonesian piped natural gas.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Over the years, Singapore has worked hard to diversify our national water taps away from an over-reliance on imported water from Malaysia to ensure a more robust and sustainable water supply.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We need to do the same for our energy supply switches.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How will the Government diversify our current 95% dependence on imported natural gas for power generation?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Clearly, we cannot afford to shift back to dirty fuels like coal and oil, which, in any case, also need to be imported.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, our future lies in greater reliance on renewable energy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The third supply switch envisions tapping on regional power grids for clean energy imports.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, the proposed import of electricity from solar farms in Australia's Northern Territory will be via undersea cables running through Indonesian waters.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This could provide the same political risks as transnational gas pipelines.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Indonesian government had to approve the undersea cable route last September and it is unclear how long this approval will be for.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Their former Prime Minister, Tun Dr Mahathir Mohamad, questioned why non-renewable energy exports to Singapore were allowed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Australian support for the export of renewable energy to Singapore may also wane with political winds.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some NUS researchers recently warned that the Australian government may suffer some pushback from its powerful coal lobby.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: On the flip side, even countries which support the development of renewables, might prefer to use that clean energy domestically to meet their own net zero pledges.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: With Singapore potentially sandwiched between competing interests that we have no control over, how will the Government manage the political risks associated with importing 30% of our electricity in the future?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: With both natural gas and electricity imports carrying risks, we need to strengthen our indigenous capabilities to produce clean energy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our geography and highly urban landscape limit our renewable energy options.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We do not have wide open deserts to set up large solar farms, but we have plenty of building rooftops and intense tropical sunlight.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: When the sun stops shining, the electrons also stop flowing.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Fortunately, battery technology has improved tremendously in recent years, driven by the growth in electric cars.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Better energy storage systems will smoothen out the imbalances between supply of and demand for solar power.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Is this really the best we can achieve with solar?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Are we planning for a large-scale deployment of solar panels on building rooftops, reservoirs and even offshore islands?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Are we providing companies sufficient incentives to boost adoption of energy storage systems that are paired with solar installations?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Besides solar energy, have we done a deep dive to explore other renewables like tidal energy, geothermal energy and offshore wind farms?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We do not have much time to diversify our energy sources away from natural gas.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As countries shut down their pollutive coal-fired power plants, natural gas will increasingly be used as a transition fuel.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will reduce the supply available to us and raise its price.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government, industry and our people need to double down to innovate and come up with more clean energy solutions to diversify our energy mix, strengthen our energy resilience and meet our current climate change pledges.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore's energy transition must be accelerated but managed well to ensure that our lights stay on and our electricity bills remain affordable.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is a timely move, as countries review and renew their climate change commitments in light of the mounting evidence of the widespread damage that climate change will have on our future generations if no action is taken.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to various scientific studies, the main driver of modern climate change comes from the burning of fossil fuels, which releases greenhouse gases that gets trapped in our atmosphere, causing the Earth to heat up.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I, therefore, fully support the proposed changes to the Electricity Act, which will allow EMA to set greenhouse gas emissions standards.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Over time, this will be an important lever for the Government to force power generation companies to use more energy-efficient technologies.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This legislative lever is especially important, given Singapore’s ambitious push, under the Singapore Green Plan, to phase out internal combustion engine vehicles by 2040 and to have all vehicles run on cleaner energy, such as electric vehicles.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But even if electric vehicles have no tailpipe emissions, they can still leave a significant carbon footprint if the source of our energy generation produces large amounts of greenhouse gases.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This puts us at a severe disadvantage during global energy crises, such as what we are facing today, which has caused wholesale electricity prices to spike.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Bill’s proposal to empower EMA to acquire, build, own and operate critical power sector infrastructure, if there is a failure in the private market, can be seen, therefore, as an important safeguard for our nation’s energy self-sufficiency should such global conditions happen again in the future.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, once the Bill is passed, EMA would have the power to act as both regulator and owner of generation companies.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: EMA would then be able to compete in the Singapore Wholesale Electricity Market and could, through the sheer financial might of the Government, dictate wholesale electricity prices.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I am, therefore, glad that the Minister has assured in his Second Reading speech earlier that the appropriate safeguards and processes will be put in place to ensure fair market competition and prevent conflicts of interest from arising.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Minister Tan See Leng spoke at length about this during yesterday’s Sitting, in response to the Parliamentary Questions filed by me and various other Members of this House.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We cannot underestimate the negative impact that this has had on affected consumers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Their contracts have been cut short and they will need to migrate to a new retailer that offers more expensive electricity plans, or have their accounts transferred back to SP Group and pay for their electricity at the regulated tariffs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The prolonged telecommuting work arrangements due to COVID-19 has also meant an increase in the average household electricity consumption during this period.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Taken together, affected consumers face a double whammy in terms of having to pay more due to higher prices and an increase in energy consumption.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Consumers have the most to lose when an electricity retailer decides to call it a day.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: That is why CASE had, in 2018, worked closely with EMA to embed consumer protection measures into the Open Electricity Market.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Consumers affected by the closures of their energy retailers will have their security deposits refunded.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They can also choose to terminate their contracts early with exiting retailers without any termination fees, before their accounts are transferred to the SP Group.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: CASE had also worked closely with EMA on consumer awareness roadshows to highlight key information, such as their consumer rights if their chosen energy retailer closes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Despite these safeguards, some consumers remain unhappy at having to suddenly pay more due to the business failures of the electricity retailers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While we cannot turn back time to shore up the poor business fundamentals of the exiting retailers, what we can do is to learn from this episode and prevent a similar exodus from happening in the future.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Markets often operate in a cycle and periods of volatile energy prices will happen again.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: What are lessons that the Ministry has learnt from this episode and how does the Ministry intend to prevent another exit of multiple electricity retailers when volatility arises once again?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Does the Ministry plan to review the mandatory hedging position by electricity retailers, particularly those who do not possess any electricity generation capabilities, and require them to hedge more aggressively so that we can avoid a repeat of an exodus of retailers when the wholesale electricity market turns volatile again?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Since its launch, retailers have been able to provide prices that are lower than the regulated tariff offered by SP Group.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But this may not necessarily always be the case.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Just like in any market, prices can rise and fall.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I started as a Technical Officer in a power generation plant and, thereafter, transited to providing consultancy and advice to Government agencies, consultants and contractors in protecting our power cables and gas pipes during the course of construction works.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The works can span from simple roadside digging to major projects like commercial buildings, even deep excavation tunnelling works.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I enjoy and take pride in doing my job for one reason: ensuring that our energy network remains uninterrupted, secure, reliable and efficient at all times.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: For the information of the House, I am the General Secretary of the Union of Power Gas Employees (UPAGE), which currently serves and represents workers in this industry.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Any change to this business model will affect our workers, either directly or indirectly.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Workers in this industry have gone through major changes since 1995, starting with the corporatisation of PUB’s electricity and gas departments into Singapore Power, currently known as SP Group.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Union leaders back then faced challenges from workers who were worried about the security of their rice bowl once they were no longer in the Government sector.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Moving forward to the late 2000s when our big generation companies were sold to foreign investors, many workers became more agitated and anxious.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The founding UPAGE leaders had to walk the ground to hear them out and give assurance that their concerns have been heard at the highest level.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This was possible because our leaders back then were closely engaged by Government leaders on the rationale for the changes in the energy business landscape.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: That laid the foundation for the strong bipartite relationship between UPAGE and the Energy Market Authority (EMA) which exists until today.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: From my earlier exchanges with management of generation companies, they have relayed to me some observations and concerns with this Bill.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: A fundamental principle of the electricity market has been the segregation of contestable and non-contestable business segments with EMA as the regulator to oversee the industry.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: A vibrant, balanced and competitive market is essential to encourage continued investment and the renewal of old assets and to provide adequate drivers to adopt new technology and improve efficiency.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In light of this, the appeal is for EMA to observe the power market for a few more years to understand if the recovery is sustained and whether private developers are investing in new capacity or repowering their ageing units.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Alternatively, if the current business model is deemed unsustainable, maybe EMA could consider revamping the market to one that is re-nationalised and carefully planned, taking a more holistic consideration of Singapore’s needs to have secure and sustainable energy supplies supported by home-grown talent.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding the above concerns, the industry players are in support of the Government’s intention to reduce carbon emissions through a long-term, low-emissions development strategy.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: They concur that this critical objective can be achieved via a multi-pronged approach, including energy efficiency enhancements, increased solar deployment, use of regional power grids for low-carbon electricity imports and the adoption of new technology.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This will then bring me to the next part of my speech on increased attention for climate change and the journey towards embarking on energy transitions and, closest to my heart, efforts to train and prepare our workforce for the future.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Many generation companies across the globe are only now shifting from coal and oil to natural gas and renewable energy sources like wind, solar and hydropower.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore, as a small city state with little natural resources and renewable energy options, has always had to rely on fuel imports to meet our energy demand.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We had, in the early 2000s, made the shift from oil to natural gas to power our electricity generators.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This was a big shift for us as a nation, as natural gas is the cleanest burning fossil fuel.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The adoption of natural gas has helped Singapore manage our carbon emissions since the switch.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: EMA has never failed to provide the necessary support and guidance on matters that relate to the business outlook that will directly affect the workforce both in the current moment and also preparing for the future.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: It is at such meetings that UPAGE was informed of this transition journey that will be undertaken by the Government to decarbonise the power grid while meeting our economy's and social energy demand via tapping on four switches, or energy supply sources, as was also announced at the 2019 Singapore International Energy Week.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In making the big shifts in energy supply, I would like to encourage industry players, especially those in the clean energy sector, to consider leveraging this transition to tap on new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I strongly encourage our Singaporeans, not just those in the power sector today, but also those who are still studying or considering a career transition, to consider joining the new and exciting opportunities in the green economy.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Closer to me, I would like to share I am blessed and grateful to be an employee of SP Group as we always believe in training our workers not just for increasing the productivity level, but also learning new skills for the future.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Since then, courses and programmes, such as Introduction to Future Grid, Energy Efficiency, requirements for installation and commissioning of Grid-Tied Photovoltaic systems, energy storage systems and more, will be introduced as we progress.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: While the Bill talks about the change of energy source security and reliability, we must not forget the manner it is brought to businesses and consumers like us.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: During the circuit breaker last year, this group of workers were either out in the hot sun or humid conditions inside the plants and stations to ensure that businesses and consumers can have a continuous and uninterrupted supply.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I hope we do not just feel upset when the tariff rates go up, but do also bear in mind the efforts of the workers that ensure our electricity and gas reach us at home.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: To all my fellow power, energy and gas sector workers, thanks for your tireless effort in this challenging time so that our fellow citizens can enjoy watching their favourite movies and cooking good and healthy food in the luxury of their homes.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Before I conclude my speech, we note that the energy transition to cleaner energy sources is but one way that we can reduce our impact on the environment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The world is gripped by an energy crisis.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The demand for natural gas has remained at multi-year highs with no clear signs of easing; the same applies for fossil fuels.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Uniform Singapore Energy Price (USEP) recorded extremely volatile intra-day figures in the past month.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This has also forced several electricity retailers out of the Open Electricity Market (OEM), so it is quite timely for us to discuss this Bill of resilience.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This Bill allows the Ministry and EMA to robustly safeguard Singapore's energy security and resilience.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, to enable EMA to acquire, build, own and/or operate critical infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Second, to empower EMA to require licensees to reduce Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Therefore, EMA must be able to address failures in the private electricity market.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The proposed amendment to empower EMA to acquire, build and own this critical infrastructure will ensure that this energy supply remains resilient.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are concerns that the EMA would potentially act both as a regulator and owner or operator of generation units.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Ministry has reiterated its commitment to ensure a competitive wholesale electricity market.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I seek the Minister's clarification on the proper governance structures to mitigate against potential conflicts of interest.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, on empowering EMA to impose requirements to reduce GHG emissions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I have spoken in this House on how critical it is to curb climate change on a few occasions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must reduce GHG emissions to the greatest extent possible.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Emissions in Singapore are largely dominated by the energy sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It accounts for 38% of the nation's carbon emissions in 2018.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Thus, to help in combatting climate change, we must lower carbon emissions by promoting energy efficiency within the energy sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The proposed amendment enables EMA, with more tools, to reduce GHG emissions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, it can introduce policies to decarbonise electricity generation and mandate the uptake of cleaner technologies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, could the Ministry clarify if EMA's efforts to reduce GHG emissions would necessarily translate into higher business costs for companies?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: If so, what are the scale and extent?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And, in turn, does it also mean higher electricity tariffs for consumers?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: If so, what is the longer-term strategy to soften this impact for consumers and businesses, especially the SMEs and lower-income households?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Second, the existing Energy Efficiency Grant for Power Generation Companies or gencos disburses grants of up to 50% of qualifying costs for gencos to invest in energy-efficient technologies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, my concern is that gencos might be constrained by the new policies while grappling with high price volatility.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: High price volatility makes it difficult for them to forecast revenue streams and apportion funds to adopt greener technology.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The quantum of the grant might be insufficient to beef up the genco's appetite to do so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to further incentivise and support gencos to switch to greener technologies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Clearly, increasing the quantum of the grant is one way but not the only one.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can also introduce flexibility tied to energy price trends.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This can allow the companies to plan and manage their cashflows better.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, on the OEM, it was introduced in 2018 and many consumers benefited from competitive pricing and innovative offers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, the price of natural gas in 2018 was half of what it is today.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This makes them less able to reap economies of scale.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It also makes it more difficult for retailers to build up financial reserves, reducing their ability to weather negative market conditions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The global energy crunch will persist for some time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The volatility will only be worsened by the shifting of investment to renewables and cleaner energy sources.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Ministry share on its plans to support these OEMs while developing a more sustainable longer-term framework?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Perhaps, there is scope to reduce the number of approved retailers to avoid disruptions to consumers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is done alongside our pursuit of combatting climate change by reducing emissions in the energy sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, there are difficult trade-offs, not the least in terms of higher costs for businesses and consumers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must develop plans to combat climate change sustainably.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Notwithstanding my clarifications and suggestions above, Mr Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's energy network, like our water network, is a critical national infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Climate change is a global emergency and a threat to mankind.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This House has committed that the Government, in partnership with the private sector, civil society and the people of Singapore, will deepen and accelerate efforts to mitigate and adapt to climate change and to embrace sustainability in the development of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The multi-Ministry Singapore Green Plan 2030, which was unveiled at Budget 2021, is an exciting vision and a rallying cry for the whole of Singapore to work towards becoming a sustainable smart nation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And Singapore has made strong commitments to reduce carbon emissions for a more sustainable future with water, food and energy being three critical pillars of our Singapore Green Plan 2030.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister has also shared in his speech that Singapore will be embarking on a multi-decade programme to transition our electricity generation to low carbon generation sources through four supply "switches".

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Government will, therefore, need to manage the transition across all of the four national "switches" while maintaining energy reliability and affordability.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill has been set out to enable EMA to implement this energy transition without disruption while ensuring the sustainability, security and reliability of the power sector.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: To ensure energy resilience, there has to be some degree of re-regulation, I suppose, even as Singapore has gone through a phase of de-regulation for a strategic resource, like electricity supply.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: To rely entirely on import for our fuel to generate electricity does have its challenges, as we have experienced.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Now, countries like Japan, after the Fukushima incident, has stocked up on gas supplies and so has China, which is now able to release gas stocks due to shortage of coal.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, while competition has helped to drive electricity prices down for a while, the recent surge in energy prices has led to the exit of many retailers and left some consumers exposed.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This is yet another example that we cannot leave it to the market to find its equilibrium for a strategic resource like electricity.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, the amendment to this Bill is timely.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The authorities have to take proactive steps to ensure energy security, including taking control of critical infrastructures and balancing market optimisation, with provisions for operational continuity and resilience.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There has been a decline in investor appetite for the building of new generation capacity as the world transitions to cleaner energy sources and the COVID-19 pandemic only makes the situation worse.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This amendment will enable EMA to ensure the reliability and resilience of our energy pillar should private sector fail to step up.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This might, of course, be viewed as a step back in an otherwise deregulated market.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I seek the Minister's indulgence that I have more questions than answers and hope that he can clarify my questions and provide a clear narrative of Singapore's strategic approach going forward to ensure energy resilience.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: First question: how will the investment of existing power generation players in Singapore be protected?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that there was a public consultation, like the Minister has mentioned.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: What were the industry's main concerns and how does the Government plan to address those concerns?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: MTI, with EDB and MOF, are extremely skilful in selling the strengths of Singapore as an investment destination and for putting together the whole of Singapore's capabilities and incentives to attract visitors to come.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Why does MTI think that the private sector may not continue to invest in this space?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: What is needed in order for Singapore to continue to be attractive for the big players in the energy space to land, expand and contribute to the building of our four supply "switches".

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is, of course, prudent for Singapore to build our capabilities if we are to ensure resilience and security in our key pillars.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We have done it for water with our four national taps, built our own capabilities in desalination as well as NEWater, amongst others, and built a strong DNA that will ensure our water resilience and security will not be threatened.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, in the wake of recent challenges with the exit of power providers, it looks to me like a timely wake-up call that we ought to be prepared to do the same for energy.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, how will Singapore plan to execute this strategy?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Do we have the skilled resources to undertake such a programme?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And lastly, how will we pacify the players in the market that there will be fair play and no unfair competition and how will we continue to attract investments in research and innovation in this whole sector?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And what is the impact on Singapore households and businesses?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding my questions, Mr Speaker, I fully support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By setting green standards, we are sending a clear signal that our commitment on sustainability towards the Singapore Green Plan 2030 is beyond rhetoric and about getting things done.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To strengthen energy resilience, the Government has a dual strategy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Second is by working closely with the generation companies to provide critical additional capacity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The adoption of this dual strategy delivers sustainable energy for Singapore and supports a viable industry that contributes to our GDP.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Notwithstanding, I would like to put forward three clarifications to this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addition, what is the remedy to these safety issues and what are the specific safety issues EMA is most concerned about?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thirdly, on the insertion of “This section   applies to any infrastructure (including cable pipe-blocks and tunnels) housing or intended to house any transmission electricity cable, as it applies to any high voltage electricity cable under the management or control of an electricity licensee…”, in section 80 of the Electricity Act, I would like to ask whether the minimum refers to high voltage, 6.6 kilovolts and 22 kilovolts, or transmission electricity cable, 66 kilovolts or higher?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addition, has MTI or EMA assessed the need to protect all above-ground access to underground infrastructure, especially since the core intention is to protect the underground infrastructure itself?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I also have three proposals for MTI’s consideration.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The district cooling system is one innovative and practical example.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is an underground centralised cooling and heating system for air-conditioning of buildings.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With district cooling, building owners need not invest in having their own chillers, thereby removing capital expenditure.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Currently, we have one at Marina Bay that is managed by SP Group and another in the upcoming Tengah development.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Ice tanks form part of a unique design feature of district cooling systems which harnesses energy to cool the ice tanks when demand is low and provides additional cooling capacity when demand is high.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This system effectively shifts the electric load requirements and optimises energy consumption throughout the day by tapering any need for energy surge or sub-optimal usage of compressors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As global temperatures are set to rise, Singapore needs to fundamentally change the way we cool spaces and scale efficient cooling systems.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Beyond implementing new innovations, such as district cooling systems in new developments and estates, we need to explore ways to implement such systems in mature business districts and residential estates.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Beyond grants, such as the district cooling grant, we should tap on private sector innovations and financing schemes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For building owners who would like to convert their existing chiller plant ownership into a utility-based cooling as a service, the private sector can offer to buy over the chiller plant from building owners and sell back chilled water as a utility.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This way, capital expenditure is avoided by leveraging on the private sector’s innovative financing model.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will help building owners’ cashflow to support their core businesses, especially during this tight economic situation, and make the transition to more sustainable consumption easier.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Separately, as we implement an energy reset, urban planning perimeters and uses should consider various energy needs throughout the day.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The peak energy needs of one activity can be curated to offset another activity through different demand periods and leading to more optimum use of energy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This could be an important new criterion for URA’s future requirements in mixed use developments.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With the maturity of digital solutions in the built environment today, there are significant opportunities to leverage on enterprise software as a service, often priced at affordable rates, with advanced fault detection and diagnostic and AI features to analyse for actionable insights and optimise energy efficiency, especially during low building occupancy, so that energy usage commensurates with the level of occupancy and activities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It can also proactively support predictive maintenance which improves plant resiliency and efficiency.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is done through smart sensing, automated response and optimisation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With its advanced features, it would also ensure the health and wellness of the built environment, supported with optimal ventilation where it is required to minimise or eradicate the infectious disease risk.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thus, it also enables clean air for the health and safety of the occupants.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The added cost benefit of such software deployment is that it involves much lesser investments compared to hardware capital expenditure.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fluctuations in energy prices affects Singapore’s cost of living and any disruptions have immense negative consequences for our industries and this puts jobs at risk.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are clear downside risks to jobs and livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we work towards reducing emissions, we need to ensure that this does not limit our economic growth.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Consequently, by investing in new taps, such as importing clean energy from regional grids, it will provide new growth opportunities and jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I believe that we can reap the benefits from building a sustainable and efficient energy system that serves our national needs while enabling us to compete globally.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: From keeping the lights on and putting food on the table, our ability to get to work or powering the devices that have become so integral in both our personal and professional lives, energy is the bedrock of what makes life powered by technology possible.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Fossil fuels have been the primary source of meeting our energy requirements for decades.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, the world has become increasingly aware about the negative environmental impacts of fuelling our energy needs primarily through fossil fuels.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How we cross over to cleaner energy matters.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Do we wait until after the switch from gas to green to make an impact?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Or do we take incremental steps to do what we can in the here and now as we make the transition.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am glad to see the Government's conviction to retiring almost all existing natural gas fuel power plants over the next one to two decades as part of our enhanced 2030 nationally-determined contributions and 2050 long-term low emissions development strategy.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have already seen some exciting ways which Singapore plans on harnessing greener energy options, such as solar energy, clean energy imports and low-carbon alternatives.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In July this year, we officially open one of the world's largest floating solar farms.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we debate this Bill, COP26 is underway in Glasgow.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am also glad that EMA will verify the cleanliness of energy inputs, including requiring proof of carbon output.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we move to ensure the importation of energy from more carbon-neutral sources, I hope that the overall supply chain in which the energy is transported here will also be taken into consideration when evaluating the reduction in carbon footprint from these efforts.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And in the same vein, I hope that we will also apply rigorous environmental and sustainability standards in the construction of the infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this Bill, I support the levers proposed to require, not just encourage, power generation companies to improve the energy efficiency of their existing units and shift towards cleaner and more efficient modes of power generation as the amendments enable EMA to implement policies, standards to require electricity generation licensees to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this regard, it would be important for EMA to start work early alongside industry for successful compliance with these standards.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to ask if EMA is planning for a transition period for such companies and, if so, how long will this be?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, the proposed amendments to have EMA build, acquire, own and operate critical power sector infrastructure if the private market fails to do is a prudent one towards safeguarding the security of our power system although I recognise that certain stakeholders are concerned that these units would compete with existing units in the Singapore wholesale electricity market with the effect of depressing wholesale electricity prices.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also support the move to allow EMA to raise capital and issue bonds as this protects our energy plans to a better degree from adverse market forces.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Few governments can or choose to fill the infrastructure investment gap alone.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With the Minister's approval, EMA will now have the ability to raise capital not just from the Government, but also any source in or outside of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think it is important for Singaporeans to be able to participate and benefit from supporting the nation's infrastructural goals.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will preference be given to Singaporeans who would like to participate in the issuance of such an infrastructure bond?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And under what conditions would EMA look to raise capital from outside of Singapore?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the event that large amounts of overseas capital are approved of and raised, will the Government make the sources of such capital public knowledge?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given the lessons we can glean now from the instability of such markets, I stand in support of the spirit of the move, but I do seek some clarity in the execution.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the instability of the energy markets, we have seen a few reports of private energy retailers closing due to rising prices.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I applaud the Government for taking the prudent step of protecting consumers' interests by drawing down on these deposits.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, many of these companies have employees, too.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And in these difficult circumstances, I would also like to ask if the Government will also consider ensuring that there is support for such employees from these companies who are choosing to downsize or exit.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The task of switching over from gas to green is a complex one and will take some time.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must pay careful consideration to ensure that while we are in transition, supply is reliable and prices are stable.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given our limitations as a small city-state, I am cognisant that we will have to straddle two walls before we can cross over the picket fence into greener pastures.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On that note, Mr Speaker, I am looking forward to the journey from gas to green with stronger compliance and standards and protection for critical infrastructure and consumers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is, indeed, timely that this Bill is introduced at a time when there is turmoil in the electricity market which has resulted in licensed retailers throwing in the towel in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The price distortions disrupted the SGX electricity futures market, leaving the retailers in the cold as they could not hedge their exposure to the price volatility triggered by the rise in gas prices overseas.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This certainly highlights the importance of Singapore ensuring that it has a strong infrastructure in place as part of our energy security.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Much has been said about going environmentally friendly and the power generation sector is certainly one big bloc.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Decarbonising electricity generation is important and the gencos need to move from fossil fuel to cleaner natural gas.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, we have to cut the amount of carbon we release into the atmosphere.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But what is important is how do we manage this migration and ensure that it does not result in a hefty burden being put on the shoulders of consumers – from households to businesses, and to Town Councils in the management of municipalities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As we know, on all fronts, costs are rising from construction, manufacturing to transportation, logistics and manpower.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have to also bear in mind that, in the near future, we would be having higher GST and other taxes to add to the cost of generating electricity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Bill highlights the strategic move for Singapore to look at imports as the most viable option for decarbonising the power generation sector in the near to medium term.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We are already importing all our energy supplies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We will have to diversify our sources of energy and importing solar power supply from Australia-Asia Power Link (AAPowerLink) is one option on the table.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another is to tap on electricity from Malaysia which is to kick-start a two-year trial starting next year to diversify the country’s energy supply.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We are also part of the Lao PDR-Thailand-Malaysia-Singapore Power Integration Project that is known as a “pathfinder” to a broader ASEAN power grid system.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will be just somewhat similar to Britain, which imports hydropower from Norway, helping to ensure secure, affordable and sustainable electricity supplies for UK consumers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Nordic power exchange, Nord Pool, held its first auction in September 2021 to trade electricity on a newly launched interconnector between Norway and Britain as both markets grapple with tight energy supplies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My first question is: in our outreach to the regional supply source and where subsea cables are needed to connect with Singapore, what does it mean for our energy infrastructure demands going forward?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How will the evolution of technology in energy infrastructure affect us and, if needed, how much would it cost in terms of actual infrastructure and human capital requirements and where would these increased landing points be located as it comes in into Singapore?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And with the need to invest in capital for the cables and the landing stations, how much more would these add to the cost for consumers, whether it is private or public built?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What can our Government do to mitigate the higher cost going forward, maybe a few decades down the road?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, could the Minister share with the House how do we ensure the reliability of the energy supply from these external sources?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In recent times, we have seen how the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted operations in some countries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, we need to think of contingencies so that we are not caught off-guard.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The resultant effect caused spot electricity futures on SGX to spike on those days.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This also prompted the operator of the LNG terminal, Singapore LNG Corp, to look into boosting gas inventory to bolster energy supplies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need to learn from this and look at how to manage such a scenario.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another question is: if we are going to build a back-up capacity, how long can it last and do we have multiple sources for this back-up?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How do we ensure, if one supply source is disrupted, the other external sources could still keep the supply flowing?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think some Members in the House mentioned this earlier, but it highlights the point that, besides diversity, we need to ensure that our external source supplies actually do not get disrupted significantly, even after diversification.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, the natural gas supply to Singapore from Indonesia was disrupted in July and, as of October, the supply has not fully recovered.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The July disruptions were blamed mainly on an unplanned shutdown at the Anoa field and planned maintenance at the Gajah Baru field, both located in Natuna, according to a report.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: EMA had also said that the disruptions in supply from Indonesia's gas fields in Natuna had contributed to a spike in our spot electricity prices. "The recent spike could be attributed to a number of factors, including higher than usual electricity demand, the outage of several generation units, curtailments of gas from West Natuna, as well as low landing pressure of the gas supplied from South Sumatra," EMA reportedly said.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The gas supply will be channelled into the Dumai Duri transmission pipeline to be distributed to industrial estates in Sumatra, namely, the Sei Mangkei Special Economic Zone in North Sumatra, among other destinations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our supply from Malaysia is also another uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is no guarantee that the expiring contract will be renewed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I believe, hence, we are moving to LNG as the alternative to fill the vacuum.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is where new offshore terminals will also add Singapore to a growing list of Asian countries deploying floating infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Minister give the House an update on this undertaking and how are we coping with these LNG alternatives?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When would LNG likely replace our demand for natural gas for use by gencos?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And what steps are in place to avoid a worst-case scenario?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
