text: Would it result in any supply shortage that may necessitate a back-out of supply to households?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At this point, if I could resurface the question whether we should consider using nuclear energy as part of our energy resilience, not within the confines of Singapore, but probably from far afield, for example.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This idea is not new and our founding Prime Minister Mr Lee Kuan Yew in 2008 had said that he had once considered tapping nuclear energy as the best alternative to fossil fuels for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Minister share his thoughts on this, please?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would this not open it to a conflict of interest?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think it would be useful if the Minister can share on this point.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This would only cause the electricity market not to be a level playing field for all participants, if you interpret it from a conflict-of-interest perspective.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Lastly, can we also know how soon EMA would be embarking on building capacity and capability to build up its expertise to handle its expanded role in the next five to 10 years, especially so when this Bill explicitly highlights the fact that EMA's powers will be extended quite largely?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I support this Bill as it has the potential to protect the day-to-day energy needs of Singaporeans and to contribute to our commitment towards fighting climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope we will continue this good practice of gathering and responding to public feedback for legislative amendments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points of clarification to make.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first clarification relates to the expansion of borrowing powers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Clause 2(a) of the Bill expands the powers of EMA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that the goal is to ensure energy security by freeing EMA to fund its construction of critical energy infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, it seems like this change also opens a gap in our energy security.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After all, borrowing from foreign financiers may also mean granting them rights and interests over parts of our energy infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What safeguards would the Ministry implement to limit the risks of foreign funding to our energy infrastructure?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second clarification is on the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In its response to feedback from the public consultation, MTI said that EMA would use its new powers under this law to develop “further targeted measures” that would reduce the power generation sector’s emissions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The latest IPCC report on climate change stresses that there is only a small window of opportunity left for countries to keep the 2050 temperature increase below two degree Celsius.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Power generators will need time to adapt to any new regulations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Ministry commit to setting an aggressive timeline for releasing EMA’s new policies?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition to sharing its timeline, will the Ministry proactively share with the public the expected emissions impact of any new power generation?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After all, as Minister Grace Fu mentioned this year, the Green Plan is a living plan, designed and executed in collaboration with our people.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let us empower members of the public to understand and support policies that will help Singapore reach its climate goals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, it does not directly deal with one of the largest global threats to energy infrastructure: cyber attacks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In 2008, an oil pipeline exploded in Turkey after cyber attackers managed to raise the pressure within the pipeline.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In 2015 and 2016, cyber attacks in Ukraine shut down electricity to hundreds of thousands of people for hours.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In May this year, a cyber attack forced the temporary shutdown of one of the US’ largest gas pipelines.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There have been many more of such attacks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We must be proactive and aggressive in closing any cybersecurity gaps in our energy infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am talking about entities across the entire supply chain, including gas pipelines, generation plants, energy retailers and more.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the Government is not able to share the specific number, can it at least confirm whether attempts at an attack have taken place?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Cyber Security Agency said in July that there had been no massive ransomware attack on our critical infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But have there been other types of attacks?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After all, some attackers may aim to cause damage rather than collect a ransom.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, will the Government update our laws to ensure high cybersecurity standards in our energy and utilities sector specifically?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Minister Josephine Teo said in October that the Government has been reviewing our cybersecurity laws.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope that this review will consider new regulations specifically for our water supply and energy supply systems.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, does the Government have plans for dealing with a successful cyber attack on our energy and water infrastructure?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Are there clear actions that would be taken on emergency supplies and crisis communications?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After all, we can do our best to build defences, but we should not pretend that a successful attack will never happen.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When it does happen, we must have contingency plans to address the unrest and emergencies that would emerge.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While logic will tell us that it is unavoidable for energy prices to rise in the short term due to a confluence of external factors, I think many would still find difficulty in understanding what we, as a nation, have to contend with in terms of the energy supply chain and its potential impact resulting in a situation of electricity shortage.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Thus, it is, indeed, timely that we are now reviewing the changes required for energy resiliency in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: For this Bill, I have three areas to raise and seek clarifications.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: First, the specifics about critical levers in the energy resilience measures.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: To enhance Singapore’s energy resilience in the longer term, it is important for us to look at it holistically from the entire value chain.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We have existing assets and infrastructures that span this value chain today.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But our challenge remains with the strong need for importation of energy sources.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I would thus like to ask which aspect will our resiliency measures moving forward be focused on: raw material sources, including green options, energy generation, the grid distribution that supports low-carbon electricity or better balancing of power allocation and usage between industries and consumers?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Given our limited land and rooftop spaces, there is a practical limit to how much we can harness from solar energy within our shores.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It is thus imperative that we look further to explore importation of renewable energy sources from other countries through regional grids.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, in the race to decarbonise each economy, neighbouring countries would have their own domestic carbon reduction commitments to achieve in the near term and may not be as forthcoming towards sale of these electricity sources to us.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Apart from Malaysia, I believe we may encounter similar situations with others.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: How then would we prepare to overcome this if Singapore’s ability to import renewable sources are limited by export measures set by other countries’ domestic considerations?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It appears that continuing to import natural gas to fulfil our usage is inevitable.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Today, it is a question about whether we have hedged sufficient supply to serve our needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Tomorrow, it will be one about whether we have the ability to offset the carbon footprint generated from these non-green fuel sources.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In my view, establishing the ground infrastructure and having a detailed transition plan to accommodate the future combination of low carbon or green fuels in our energy generation and distribution system are fundamental.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: These infrastructure projects are extremely costly and the appropriate choice of technology selected at any point will give rise to future impact on sufficiency in supply while also having to meet the evolving and higher bars of climate change goals.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: On this note, I would like to ask the Minister in the case that we switch to lower carbon sources, for example, hydrogen, this would mean some changes are required for the pipelines and electricity grids.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: There is also a likelihood for more public-private partnership to involve the local players and overseas companies with the expertise to enable adoption of microgrid supplies as we transition to prevent any disruption.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Second, the impact on Smart Nation status for businesses and prioritisation for energy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The transition towards being a Smart Nation and an attractive industry or business hub for global players to form a base in Singapore is an energy-intensive play and one with a long tail.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Having said that, I belong to the school of thought that we should pursue this aspiration and continue to strengthen our ability to support these industries as they set foot on our shore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, I feel that the path to evolve is one where the industry players and businesses here must take an active role in shaping and contributing their share of reducing energy needs and, concurrently, using technologies to enable adaptation of their facilities for usage of greener energy sources or to decarbonise existing infrastructures.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: If not, will further actions be taken to address them so as to ensure balanced stability in energy consumption over time?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Moving on, let me raise the point about consumption pattern and energy allocation of power supply.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As a resource-constrained nation, we are resigned to the fact about our predominant need for energy imports.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Yet, I believe it is ever so important for us to be more intentional and conscious with regard to our energy usage and allocation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As a manufacturing hub for higher value-add technologies and digitalisation, some services like data centres, foundries and green fuels will bring benefits to our broader ecosystem.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Has COVID-19 changed some of this and the new way of work?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It warrants some hard look at the fresh data.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Lastly, the longer-term plans for Singapore’s decarbonisation of energy sources.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Diversification has long been a cornerstone of Singapore’s public policy on resources, be it water or energy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It would be helpful if the Minister can shed more insights on our plans in this area.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Notwithstanding the above raised, I support the Bill, as it is crucial for us to plan ahead on critical elements for future implementation and laying the path for our ability to adapt and change to cater to the ever-growing need for energy.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This is coupled with the energy crunch in natural gas and the recent rising cost of Brent crude.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As a country, we must be keenly aware that we import our energy and we must compete with the rest of the world for our energy resource.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: But this ability to purchase and secure energy is only a short-term measure.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We are facing the dawn of the next energy transition.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As we rebalance our carbon-based energy, we are faced with several critical decision points to secure our energy for the future.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I have a few questions for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: With this amendment, how will the agency better plan the new energy transition that we will face in the near future?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How are we building new capabilities and rebalancing our reliance on fossil energy?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: What is the future for hydrogen, nuclear fission and fusion to provide safe, reliable and clean energy to power the country and our industrious Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The key to any energy transition plan concerning any new energy – for example, hydrogen, nuclear energy, be it fission or fusion – we must develop a clear understanding of the limitations of physics, engineering limitations and, finally, perhaps most importantly, supply chain constraints, both in materials, fuel cycles and operational implementation.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I will not go into the details of solar, wind, geothermal, green, blue, grey hydrogen, the intricacies of tritium, deuterium or super-conducting magnetic tapes.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Critically, we must see past the hype, drill down to the basics and avoid oversimplification.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must be technically strong to analyse and interpret new technologies.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must be cognisant of the engineering challenges to build, operate and manage a safe, viable, resilient and sustainable system; above all, a system that contributes to the fight against climate change.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I trust that this Bill will provide the ability to build capabilities to secure new sources of energy and for our future.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members have raised very good clarifications and suggestions which fall into four broad categories.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The first category is on energy security and resilience, including the amendments to enable EMA to build, own and operate critical power infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Second, the amendments to enhance protection of critical electricity and gas infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Third, provisions to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and enhance the environmental sustainability of the energy sector.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And, finally, the impact of the energy transition on electricity prices.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Before I address these issues, I would like to thank Mr Melvin Yong, Mr Gerald Giam, Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Mr Shawn Huang, for their questions and suggestions about the Open Electricity Market or OEM.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As I mentioned yesterday, the OEM remains viable but safeguards may need to be strengthened.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are very mindful of the higher electricity bills that households and businesses will be facing.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is what I also shared yesterday in my response to the whole series of Parliamentary Questions that were brought up and also the supplementary questions that were directed at us.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will work with MOF to review and assess if more support is needed.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: My Ministry and EMA will study this closely and we will provide further updates when ready.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Gerald Giam asked about the measures to enhance the security and resilience of our energy supply.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: During Question Time yesterday, I spoke at length about the actions that Singapore is taking to safeguard our energy security amidst the ongoing global energy crisis.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I will now touch on how we can ensure energy security over a longer term.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: From 2013, we have supplemented Piped Natural Gas (PNG) with imported Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG).

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have been ramping up solar energy production locally and we are now one of the most solar-dense cities in the world.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, as I have said many times, solar energy alone will not be sufficient to meet our energy needs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I do not think we can wait till 2050.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Even if we are able to harness all of that maximum solar potential, it would only roughly provide about 10% of our future energy needs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, regardless of the measures that we take through solar power adoption locally, we will still have to import significant renewable electricity from the region.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are also developing and trialling new low-carbon alternatives, like hydrogen, as options for the longer term.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I will speak and elaborate more on this later.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Second, beyond diversifying the types of energy that we use, we will also diversify the geographical sources of energy to manage our energy risks.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This will be an important consideration in EMA's request for proposals (RFPs) for electricity imports.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Miss Cheryl Chan asked about the impact of Malaysia's ban on renewable energy exports to Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Singapore lies in a region that has abundant renewable energy potential.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For example, Indonesia has geothermal and solar power potential.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Thailand, Vietnam and the Lao PDR also have good wind and hydropower potential.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Beyond that, Australia is also a possible source.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We welcome all companies which are keen to collaborate on the development of renewable energy sources to participate in EMA's requests for proposal for electricity imports.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Every source of energy has a risk of disruption.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: When we start to import electricity and harness more solar energy, we will also need to have sufficient amounts of other types of back-ups, including energy storage systems and generators.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We plan to work with the private sector to build the necessary infrastructure to diversify and secure our energy supply.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, as Mr Liang Eng Hwa pointed out, what we need may not necessarily be what private investors are able or willing to provide.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Should this happen, we must be prepared to provide the infrastructure to ensure energy security and reliability for ourselves.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Thus, we are moving legislation to empower EMA to acquire, build, own, and/or operate critical infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, this is a very important and critical point.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Mr Gerald Giam, Mr Abdul Samad, Mr Melvin Yong and Ms Janet Ang have asked how EMA intends to level the playing field between private investments and those that are built, owned and/or operated by EMA.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For a start, EMA will ensure that these infrastructures are subject to the same stringent standards and requirements as their private counterparts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: EMA will put in place governance structures and, if necessary, separate subsidiaries to mitigate conflicts of interest and ensure accountability.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Nevertheless, I would like to reiterate that our preference has been, and continues to be, for the private sector to provide and operate the critical infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We remain committed to facilitating private sector investments in the energy sector.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I agree with Mr Shawn Huang that these amendments must benefit the business and household consumers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In the event that EMA needs to intervene and provide the critical infrastructure and services needed, EMA will coordinate closely with industry stakeholders to avoid duplicative investments.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Miss Cheryl Chan asked if there are particular aspects that we will focus on to enhance the resilience of our energy sector.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The energy sector is a complex network of integrated systems.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Every component will need to function well to keep the lights on.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Besides ensuring access to energy sources, we also need to progressively upgrade and enhance our grid infrastructure to support rising electricity demand and a more complex power system with diverse and distributed sources of low-carbon energy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are also conducting testbeds on microgrids to assess their feasibility and ability to enhance grid resilience.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Louis Ng has pointed out other threats to energy security, such as cybersecurity and foreign influence.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: My Ministry and EMA, are fully aware of these risks and we have put in place safeguards to address them.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On the cyber health of our energy system, there have not been any successful cyber attacks on Singapore's critical energy installations thus far, but we are not resting on our laurels.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: EMA has detected a few spoofing and phishing attempts targeting companies in the energy sector in the past few years, but these attacks were on IT and Non-Critical Information Infrastructure, or non-CII, networks.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The spoofing and phishing attempts were also quickly contained and addressed.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The operation of critical infrastructure, such as our gas and electricity systems, facilities, plants and equipment, was not affected.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Nonetheless, as I have said, we are not complacent and we take cybersecurity threats very seriously.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Electricity and Gas Acts and the Computer Misuse and Cybersecurity Act give EMA and the Cyber Security Agency, or CSA, the mandate to address cybersecurity threats.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: EMA has developed a cybersecurity governance framework for the energy industry, in partnership with CSA.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is in line with the reporting requirements for Government agencies with critical infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: EMA also organises regular industrywide exercises and sharing sessions to ensure the sector's resilience and readiness in emergency responses to cyber attacks.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: EMA will continue to work with CSA and the industry to ensure the robustness and relevance of our cybersecurity governance framework.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is the same for our water supply infrastructure, with a clear framework and regular exercises in place.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On foreign influence through financing, EMA will ensure that the expanded borrowing powers to issue bonds do not compromise the security of our energy system.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As a general principle, any borrowing by EMA to fund energy infrastructure will not be securitised to the asset.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: When entering into loan agreements with financial institutions, EMA will also ensure that lenders do not have the ability to influence decisions relating to the energy infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Bill will make it an offence to damage protective infrastructure housing transmission electricity cables that are 66 kilovolts and above.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These are high-voltage transmission cables that serve more customers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Damage to these cables will thus have a greater impact on our electricity supply to consumers and businesses.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This Bill also clarifies the existing role of SP Services Ltd, the market support services licensee or provider, in carrying out safety inspections of electrical installations in premises to ensure safe and continued operations.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This includes testing to confirm that the devices operate as intended and ensuring that the electrical socket outlets are not installed near any water point.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The inspections are arranged by the licensed electrical worker engaged by the owner of the premises, with the consent of the owner of the premises.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Several Members have also spoken about the importance of ensuring the environmental sustainability of the energy sector.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We agree that this is very important and we are committed to decarbonising the power sector.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Enabling EMA to require licensees to reduce greenhouse gas emissions is an important step.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In response to Mr Liang Eng Hwa's suggestions, EMA will use a combination of broad-based regulatory measures and targeted support measures to encourage the whole industry to decarbonise.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Louis Ng and Ms Nadia Samdin asked about our timelines for imposition of new greenhouse gas emissions standards.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In developing greenhouse gas emissions standards, EMA will ensure that these standards are reasonable and realistic, but they are also ambitious.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The public can monitor our progress in decarbonising the power grid via the Grid Emissions Factor report, or the GEF report, which EMA publishes on its website very year.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Desmond Choo and Mr Melvin Yong asked about incentives to encourage the adoption of more energy- and carbon-efficient technologies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is equivalent to taking about 15,000 cars off the roads annually.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Earlier this year, EMA launched the second grant call.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: EMA will review and calibrate the level of grants based on the carbon abatement potential of the projects.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But all of these efforts alone are not sufficient.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will need to continue to explore new energy solutions to meet our long-term energy needs and low-emission targets.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Miss Cheryl Chan, Ms Janet Ang, Mr Shawn Huang and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about our efforts to develop low-carbon alternatives, such as carbon capture, utilisation and storage capabilities, hydrogen and nuclear technologies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Government is investing heavily in research and development efforts and collaborating with like-minded international partners to understand the potential for deploying these low carbon technologies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, many countries are investing heavily in lowering the cost of producing, transporting, storing and using hydrogen.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: MTI and EMA are also actively exploring low-carbon sources of energy which can be produced in Singapore, including geothermal energy, and accelerating the deployment of solar energy, notwithstanding the limited potential that we have.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As for nuclear energy, while there have been advancements in nuclear reactor technologies which have the potential to improve the safety of nuclear generation, many of these are still in the research and development phase and they have not begun commercial operations.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, we will continue to monitor the progress of these technologies, while also strengthening our capabilities to understand nuclear science and technology to assess the implications for Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will need to carefully calibrate our transition to manage its impact on energy security and reliability.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the same time, we will also need to press on with our energy conservation efforts and find ways to use energy more efficiently.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I would also like to thank Mr Edward Chia for his many insightful suggestions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Besides technologies and systems, another critical ingredient for the energy transition is human capital.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat would be pleased to hear that EMA has been updating and strengthening its capabilities to keep pace with the changing energy landscape over the years, through capability sharing platforms with industry stakeholders and foreign regulators.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: EMA is also working closely with the Union of Power and Gas Employees to implement upskilling and reskilling courses to empower the workforce with the necessary skills required to support the transition.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And I am heartened to hear from Mr Abdul Samad that these courses and programmes have been well-received.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On electricity costs, Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Desmond Choo have also raised concerns about electricity costs associated with the energy transition, including for electricity imports.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is an inevitable and necessary trade-off to address climate change.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: EMA will continue to work closely with industry partners to explore and develop cost-competitive and secure solutions that will meet both our long-term energy needs and low-emissions targets.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the same time, the Government will continue to provide targeted support for vulnerable households to help them cope with higher electricity costs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: My colleagues and I remain committed to building on this strong foundation, working closely with our industry and with our union partners.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This Bill will ensure that EMA, Electricity and Gas Acts continue to remain relevant and effective, empowering EMA with the necessary levers to navigate the energy transition while safeguarding Singapore’s energy security, reliability and affordability.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Was this study based on current solar technology or did it include projections for future improvements in the technology?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I am asking this question because I just want to be sure that the Government does not limit its expectations of the potential of solar energy on account of this study alone because technology will improve over time and the viability of solar has improved tremendously in recent years and could improve much further in the years to come.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, we are not tied down to a particular ratio in our energy mix.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But moving forward, we are going to continue to explore and pursue all of these R&D initiatives relentlessly to become more and more self-sufficient.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.50 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.25 pm until 4.50 pm.
